The Commission and the Council must remain vigilant and insistent on tangible progress.
reason: Demands concrete reforms in Kosovo, a fight against organized crime and trafficking, and protection of minority rights, showing clear policy preferences.

en: We have established that in Kosovo – the third state that receives the most aid from the European Union – there are extremely worrying cases of corruption with grave consequences for the certainty of our budget and the financial interests of the Community. We await an explanation. There is currently no one representing our interests on this matter.
reason: Points out corruption in EU aid to Kosovo and calls for accountability, but lacks a broader ideological principle beyond fiscal oversight.

en: The vote will take place on Thursday, 5 February 2009.
reason: Provides only a factual statement about a voting date, with no political principle or ideological content.

en: What are our fellow citizens expecting today? The car industry, as you said, employs 12 million people in the European Union and is equal to 10% of GDP. If I did not fear being politically incorrect, I would add that the requirements placed on the car industry and the encouragement not to use vehicles are also contributing to this situation. It is essential, in the first instance, that the banking system lends normally to the car industry, that is to say at normal rates and conditions and at volumes corresponding to the needs of that industry. We must enter tomorrow’s world and speed up the necessary developments with regard to the protection of the environment and the requirements of sustainable development in particular.
reason: Advocates for favorable banking conditions for the car industry while also stressing environmental sustainability, indicating a mixed economic‑environmental policy stance.

en: I have seen one estimate saying that 2 million jobs could potentially be lost in the course of the year in the car industry as a whole, the majority of which would be in the parts sector.
reason: Mentions a projected job loss in the car sector without offering policy recommendations or ideological judgment.

en: In my view, the appalling drop in the latest registrations – in some Member States this month they are down 33%, or 20%, and so on – shows that the crisis is not in a technologically obsolete sector, nor is it an internal crisis caused by managerial errors in this or that company. It is a systemic crisis, and as such must be tackled urgently and decisively by the European institutions. However, while this consumption support measure is implemented, which is a medium-term measure, I think we have to say that we need immediate credit support to recommence production, pay for materials and retain employees despite the fall in orders and demand.
reason: Advocates immediate EU‑level credit support and decisive intervention by European institutions to rescue the car industry, reflecting a clear stance on market regulation and supranational economic policy.

en: I have no doubt that the financial crisis will give rise to significant corrections in the future structure of the car market.
reason: Only predicts structural changes in the car market without endorsing any political principle or policy direction.

en: We would be making a big mistake if, with our economic measures, we were to pursue goals relating to climate protection and energy security as unambitious as those we have laid down in the regulation of CO for cars. It is my belief that we really must aim to make it clear to the carmakers that the future of cars lies in small, efficient and climate-friendly models and that every effort must be made, in connection with incentive measures, to promote such models. However, this is only possible in conjunction with a coordinated plan involving energy policy.
reason: Calls for climate‑friendly, small efficient cars and coordinated energy policy, showing a strong commitment to environmental regulation and market transformation.

en: Labour must then be restored to its central place in Europe, to play its due role as the founder of democracy.
reason: Calls for labour to be restored to a central role in Europe as the foundation of democracy, expressing a clear pro‑labour, democratic principle.

en: What are we going to do when the Americans, as the dollar is falling, sell their gas-guzzling, subsidised and highly promoted 4x4s on our market, which is also under siege from bottom-of-the-range vehicles from Turkey, India and China? We must re-establish the common external tariffs abolished by the Maastricht Agreements. However, as you know, Protocol 27 and Article 63 of the Treaty of Lisbon strictly prohibit any customs protection of the European market.
reason: Advocates re‑establishing common external tariffs (protective customs measures) despite EU treaty constraints, indicating a clear protectionist stance on trade policy.

en: Of course, we live in the real world, however, and following a 5% fall in vehicle production over the last year, the industry is expecting a further 15% fall in 2009. That is the biggest fall in the European Union since 1993 and will mean 3.8 million fewer vehicles than in 2007. It is important to realise that for every job that is held in the motor industry itself there are another five in associated areas and industries that depend on it. That means that the financial crisis, clearly, has a particularly heavy impact on the automotive sector, as it affects both the manufacturers themselves and their customers. The point has been made that the motor industry has access to EUR 9 billion from the European Investment Bank. However, both manufacturers and suppliers do need further credit in order to finance their businesses and so, too, do customers if they are to finance the purchase of cars. We therefore need to put our foot on the accelerator in order to shore up demand, as European passenger car registrations fell by 19% in quarter 4 of 2008, while those for commercial vehicles fell by 24%. These losses – especially in the light of the 2 million stockpiled vehicles – are based on significant falls in the book value of leasing vehicles which then lead to problems in this respect, too.
reason: Emphasises the need for additional credit and EU‑backed financing to sustain the automotive sector, reflecting support for state‑driven economic assistance.

en: Nissan’s Sunderland plant is widely acknowledged as the most productive in Europe. It needs to be urgently simplified and mobilised on a massive scale as part of a coordinated European response to the crisis in the car industry.
reason: Urges a coordinated European response to simplify and mobilise production, signalling a preference for EU‑wide intervention in the industry.

en: The crisis in the car industry is not a purely economic crisis. If we are now to make billions of taxpayers’ money available, the terms must be clear. In Germany, if the CEO of Deutsche Bank, Josef Ackermann, decides to scrap his nine year-old third, fourth or fifth car and buy a new Porsche Cayenne, he will receive EUR 4 000.
reason: Criticises the use of taxpayers’ money for luxury purchases, reflecting a fiscal‑responsibility stance but without a broader policy framework.

en: The EU has for a long time required a one-sided flexibility from workers. The lack of flexibility and new thinking has, after all, contributed to the crisis we are seeing in the car industry and in other industries.
reason: Blames lack of worker flexibility for the crisis, implying a position on labour‑market reforms, though the statement is relatively vague.

en: One of the statistics from our summit – from Professor David Bailey in our Birmingham Business School – estimates that 300 000 consumers in the United Kingdom were refused a car credit application over the last six months.
reason: Provides a statistic about credit refusals without linking it to any political principle or policy proposal.

en: This concerns not only the large car firms, but also all businesses associated with the car industry. I therefore believe that swift, assured and realistic intervention is needed, and I know that Mr Verheugen will be attentive and sympathetic. We must act immediately to review the criteria of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund to be used to support European workers, and I believe that more funding is needed, from ...
reason: Advocates EU‑wide, swift intervention and increased funding of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund to protect workers – a clear stance on social protection and redistribution at the EU level.

en: Every Member State is doing its own thing and launching national support measures. There are Member States – as you know better than we do – that promise cheap loans for car manufacturers, provided that these car manufacturers buy parts from local suppliers in that country.
reason: Criticises fragmented national support measures and implies a preference for coordinated policy, but does not explicitly state a concrete principle or preferred structure.

en: Therefore, I would like to put forward four proposals.
reason: Only announces forthcoming proposals without presenting any ideological content or political principle.

en: In Romania, for example, there are more than 400 companies involved in producing car components, which achieved a total turnover in 2008 of EUR 8 billion. Bearing in mind the large number of employees within these companies, I feel that car component and tyre manufacturers must be included in any future solution for providing economic support during this crisis.
reason: Calls for inclusion of car component manufacturers in future economic support programmes, signalling a clear position on EU‑level economic assistance and sectoral solidarity.

en: I believe that this would represent an economic programme through which the Council could show, as one – as this would have to be decided unanimously – how consumption-based vehicle taxes could be brought on-line. In such an event, would the Commission act harmoniously to find a European solution for General Motors’ subsidiaries?
reason: Calls for consumption‑based vehicle taxes and unanimous Council decisions, advocating harmonised EU fiscal policy and coordinated action for GM subsidiaries.

en: The German Government, in addition to supporting German manufacturers, has decided to assist vehicle users. Anyone who decides to send their old car to the scrap yard will receive EUR 2500. Without calling into question the principles behind the action taken to aid the car manufacturing industry in Europe, I would like to once again remind you of how painfully unfair the European Commission’s decision, namely that State aid given by the Polish Government to Polish shipyards must be repaid, was. As a result of this decision, around 50 000 jobs are now being cut in the Polish ship-building sector itself, while over ten thousand jobs will be lost in related industries in the future.
reason: Opposes the European Commission’s state‑aid ruling on Polish shipyards, labeling it unfair and highlighting job losses – a strong stance on state aid rules and national economic sovereignty.

en: The protective measures proposed by some states are no way to tackle the current crisis. Through funding research and development, through supporting investment...
reason: Rejects protective national measures and promotes EU‑funded research, development and investment, expressing a clear preference for coordinated economic policy over isolated national actions.

en: Above all, Commissioner, thank you for saying that we should allow our manufacturers to be more flexible through less regulation, less law and less exorbitant bureaucracy.
reason: Explicitly supports deregulation – less law, less bureaucracy – to give manufacturers flexibility, a clear ideological commitment to market liberalisation.

en: This procedure was introduced in order to invigorate our debates, to generate dialogue with the Commission and to strengthen the debating culture.
reason: Speaks only about procedural improvements to debate and dialogue; lacks a substantive political principle or policy prescription.

en: The Government of Malta is claiming that reimbursement will amount to millions of Euros. This is such a serious blunder that if it happened in any other member state of the EU, the Government would have been forced to resign. In Malta the Government has not even had the decency to accept responsibility and apologize to the thousands of Maltese and Gozitans who have been affected.
reason: Calls for government accountability and apology in Malta, indicating a weak normative stance on political responsibility but without a broader ideological framework.

en: It accounts for 3% of the EU’s GDP and generates a commercial surplus of EUR 35 billion. One job in a car company is linked to another four jobs at suppliers and another five in related sectors and sales. It is therefore clear that the health of this sector of the European economy is vital to the EU economy as a whole.
reason: The statement only describes the economic importance of a sector for the EU; it does not advocate any political principle or policy change.

en: However, we are waiting with a great deal of interest for legally binding proposals. However, I consider it extremely important that it should be clear how European citizens on the scene of a crisis are to be informed as to who is the Lead State.
reason: Calls for legally binding proposals and clear information to citizens in crises, indicating support for rule‑of‑law, transparency and structured EU crisis management.

en: Member States have a duty to put an end to this situation. It is necessary to make guidelines binding and to make information available to citizens. The Union must start negotiations with third countries in order to ensure the necessary diplomatic protection.
reason: Advocates that Member States have a duty, that guidelines be binding, information be available, and the Union negotiate for diplomatic protection—clear stance on governance and external policy.

en: Outside the Union, we are just 27 States, 27 administrations, 27 flags and 27 consular systems, or in some cases, not even that. As Europeans, they do not exist outside the European Union.
reason: Criticises the EU’s fragmented external representation but does not explicitly propose a principle; only a weak ideological signal.

en: During the Slovenian Presidency of the European Union, France represented the European Union in many countries, such as Asia, Africa and Latin America, as Slovenia had no embassies in those places. reason: Raises concern about whether citizens of smaller Member States would receive adequate consular assistance, implying a position on equal treatment within the EU.

en: Of course, there needs to be a criterion as to when and how other consular services should become involved, and these break down basically into three. reason: Describes procedural criteria for consular services without advocating any change or principle; merely informational.

en: The problem is in the very wording, in the fundamentals of Article 20 itself. You cannot go to countries such as India or to Latin American countries – there are many other countries where a presence is required in such a critical place as Mumbai – and then have only a small number of staff and inadequate security structures. That is why it is important that the Council and the Commission undertake a careful analysis of this issue.
reason: Calls for careful analysis of staffing and security under Article 20, indicating a policy position on EU external representation and safety.

en: We cannot even actually agree on what Article 20 means. We will surely not make progress, unless it is legally confirmed that it is a right with binding EU decisions and common standards and the right to challenge a refusal of protection in the courts.
reason: Strongly demands legally binding rights, common standards and the ability to challenge refusals in court—clear commitment to rule‑of‑law and supranational authority.

en: I wonder whether the Presidency and the Council understand the worthlessness of this document in Member States. I know of another Member – a British Member – who had difficulty in Dublin. We really need to bring home to our own Member States that this is a travel document of Parliament, the Commission and of the Union and should be fully respected. I would ask you to take that up with each of the Member States and ensure that it is implemented, because that sort of protection should extend to officials and to Members of Parliament travelling on the business of Parliament.
reason: Advocates that the parliamentary travel document be fully respected and protected across Member States, supporting institutional rights within the Union.

en: I would just say from experience that, without going into stories, I would like to see more coordination, more help between embassies in the bigger countries where they do have embassies and consuls in almost every country, so as to help all other Member State embassies with their constituents.
reason: Urges greater coordination between embassies to assist constituents, reflecting a stance on improved consular cooperation and citizen assistance.

en: In practice, this means that, while staying in a third country where the Member State of which he is a citizen has no representation, all EU citizens have the right to diplomatic and consular protection from any of the other Member States, according to the same principles as the citizens of that country. Unfortunately, the critical situation in Mumbai following the bombings last year revealed the shortcomings of many diplomatic offices, in terms of the practical application of Community decisions concerning the security of EU citizens. The Member States should do all that they can to ensure that it is properly implemented, and guarantee equal treatment and care to all EU citizens.
reason: Advocates that EU Member States must ensure proper diplomatic protection and equal treatment for all EU citizens, expressing a clear principle about citizens' rights and EU integration.

en: The conduct of the diplomats of some Member States in Mumbai did not only violate the rights of the EU citizens, but also pointed out deficiencies in the EU integration process. Therefore, it is crucially important for the EU to investigate this particular case and take action to ensure that such a situation does not occur again. I would appreciate it, if the Council and the Commission could assure that the implementation of Article 20 of the Treaty is closely monitored and that every deviation is investigated thoroughly.
reason: Calls for EU investigation and monitoring of Article 20 to address deficiencies in the EU integration process, explicitly supporting stronger EU oversight and citizen protection.

en: I was concerned, though, that the consultation period for that finished at the end of August, just before the real financial crisis hit.
reason: Only remarks on timing of a consultation period; no political principle or policy stance is expressed.

en: This plan is providing a sum of EUR 30 billion for small- and medium-sized enterprises.
reason: States a funding amount for SMEs without advocating any ideological position or principle.

en: Does the Council Presidency have any information that the BRIC countries, as a result of the commitments made in Washington, may be disposed to adopt a more active role and contribute to the successful outcome of the Doha Round?
reason: Poses a factual question about BRIC countries and Doha Round; lacks any expressed political principle.

en: In November the Commission proposed a revision of the directive on the energy efficiency of buildings.
reason: Mentions a Commission proposal without endorsing or opposing the policy; no clear ideological commitment.

en: What can the Council do to implement this solution? Can the Council inspire the European Technology Institute in Budapest to address itself to the problem of the energy efficiency of buildings?
reason: Asks what the Council can do to promote energy‑efficiency of buildings, hinting at support for regulation but remains a vague request without a strong stated principle.

en: I refer specifically to discussions with partners to the east over strategic energy corridors which could serve to guarantee the EU's energy security and economic competitiveness into the future.
reason: Advocates strategic energy corridors to guarantee EU energy security and competitiveness, clearly expressing a policy priority for EU energy strategy.

en: We all agree they need all the help they can get: nicotine replacement therapies etc.
reason: Expresses generic agreement about needing nicotine replacement therapies; no political principle is articulated.

en: The next item is the Commission statement on the dramatic consequences of the ‘Klaus’ storm in Southern Europe.
reason: Simply notes a commission statement on a storm; contains no ideological content or policy stance.

en: In November 1999, I took the floor in this very Chamber following the storm which had raged in south-west France, to call for European solidarity when wide-scale natural disasters lay waste to our countries. Ten years ago I was told that there was no European fund to help our fellow citizens in such times of need.
reason: Explicitly calls for European solidarity and a EU fund to aid disaster‑stricken countries, a clear stance on EU‑level collective action.

en: It is an understatement to say that Europe was not prepared to endure such a tragedy again, so soon. On 24 and 25 January this year, storm Klaus, which hit southern Europe, killed 11 people in France, 14 in Spain and three in Italy. I therefore hope, although you have just said so, that the Commission will take this message on board and mobilise all means necessary to respond to this urgent situation, in particular through the EU Solidarity Fund and the Civil Protection Financial Instrument. Lastly, in conclusion, I would like to remind you that, as with the fires in Greece in 2007, this violent storm has demonstrated the need for a civil protection force that can be mobilised in all crisis areas.
reason: Advocates that the European Commission should mobilise the EU Solidarity Fund and a civil‑protection force, directly endorsing EU institutional response.

en: I remember in the Committee on Budgets, when we discussed funds, precisely for the climate, we were talking about a few tens of millions of euros. This storm alone has cost EUR 1.4 billion. How much will we have to pay in insurance bills before we realise that protection of the environment and the climate is not a burden, but an investment in the future? But we already said that, as I recall, here in this Chamber following the AZF factory explosion in my city, in 2001.
reason: Frames climate protection as an investment and links disaster costs to the need for environmental policy, expressing a pro‑climate, EU‑action principle.

en: Apart from lamenting the loss of so many irreplaceable human lives and expressing our solidarity with the families in their grief, the European Union must act, as it has on other occasions, by mobilising either the Solidarity Fund or another more appropriate fund, to repair the material damage caused by this natural disaster.
reason: States that the EU must act by using the Solidarity Fund to repair damage, a direct endorsement of EU disaster‑relief mechanisms.

en: There are victims in France and Spain and this evening we think of them and their families. 200 000 hectares of forest have been destroyed in the south west of France. In fact, this storm has ravaged 60% of the Landes forest. Many roads are still impassable due to obstacles such as fallen trees, power lines, floods or landslips. The Commission has already announced a Communication on adapting to climate change.
reason: Mainly descriptive; only mentions a Commission communication on climate adaptation without a clear policy demand.

en: This is the third catastrophic storm in 20 years. The reason I remember it is that I live in Gironde, very close to the Gironde forests. Finally, I would like the European Union Solidarity Fund to be mobilised.
reason: Simple but explicit request for mobilisation of the European Union Solidarity Fund, showing support for EU‑wide aid.

en: The storm caused injuries and badly damaged homes, infrastructure, farms, businesses, industrial plant, sports facilities as well as public and municipal buildings. As we know and as has been mentioned here, on 26 January the two worst affected Member States, France and Spain, requested European aid for the damage caused by the storm.
reason: Proposes creating a hardship fund within the CAP, advocating specific EU agricultural policy reforms.

en: Perhaps we need to look at funding under rural development or the common agricultural policy and establish a hardship fund to look after cases like this which are there and which need assistance.
reason: Describes personal involvement in a Commission‑funded project; lacks a clear policy advocacy or ideological claim.

en: Almost all of the people who died were either disabled or elderly and in nursing homes or residential care, or in respite while their families were on holiday. I have spoken to many people in France about this incident, as I am involved in the Commission-funded project on rescuing people with disabilities in disasters.
reason: Notes the usefulness of the Solidarity Fund and cites a past payment, providing some endorsement but limited explicit advocacy.

en: In Slovakia, we watched our television screens with feelings of profound sympathy as the terrible tragedy unfolded in the village of Sant Boi de Llobregat where four children lost their lives after the roof was blown off a sports hall. The Solidarity Fund is a useful instrument. Following the November 2004 storm which destroyed 2.5 million cubic metres of timber, Slovakia received EUR 5,667,578 from this fund.
reason: References the Solidarity Fund as a useful instrument and reports past aid, showing moderate support for EU aid mechanisms.

en: I think we need to look again at regulation. The difficulty is that, back in 1999, when we discovered a problem in Belgium, we thought then that we had tightened up our rules sufficiently so that there would not be another incident. That is why I think that tonight’s debate is not just about Ireland. In my view, it is clear from your statement that this problem that occurred in Ireland has the potential to happen in other Member States.
reason: Advocates revisiting and strengthening EU regulation to prevent similar incidents, showing a clear stance on market regulation and EU oversight.

en: Indeed, unfortunately, Ireland was one of those Member States which had to be forced by threats of legal action to actually implement this directive, five years later, in 2001. Of course, the process of implementing it is still, it would appear, under way, and the inspection procedures for ensuring that it is being complied with appear to be quite weak. I have two questions for the Commissioner. Should we not be looking more seriously at taking these PCBs out of circulation much more quickly than is envisaged, particularly because of the late way in which many Member States actually implemented the directive?
reason: Calls for stricter and faster enforcement of the PCB directive and stronger inspection procedures, expressing a firm position on environmental regulation and EU law implementation.

en: That industry is valued at approximately EUR 1 billion and is responsible, directly and indirectly, for the employment of 10 000 people. Against the backdrop of the current economic climate and the rising cost of food prices, it is critical that we do our utmost in Ireland to defend the Irish pigmeat sector, which operates to the highest European Union and international standards. While any contamination of our food is always regrettable, what this incident shows is the very high level of food safety controls which the Irish authorities have in place to guarantee the integrity of the food chain.
reason: Defends existing high food‑safety standards and praises the current system, offering a mild endorsement of consumer‑safety policy but without a clear call for change.

en: In my view, we have at least two problems. On a final note, I hope that this debate will give us some answers, at least to these two questions.
reason: Only mentions having problems and hoping for answers; no explicit political principle or policy recommendation is presented.

en: First of all, we must underline that the problem does not stem from some animal disease but from the inadequate monitoring of stipulated measures carried out for fodder hygiene and safety in the European Union. reason: Explicitly urges the European Commission to adopt stronger legislation and monitoring for fodder safety, a clear advocacy for EU‑wide consumer‑protection regulation.

en: All of us – Parliament, the decreasing number of farmers and also consumers – expect the proper application of EU legislation with inspections to that effect.
reason: Expresses expectation that EU legislation be properly applied with inspections, supporting rule‑of‑law and enforcement of EU policy.

en: And, above all, and this is my last point, will you ensure that such a problem can never again occur?
reason: Requests guarantees that the problem will not recur, implying support for preventive measures, but lacks a specific policy articulation.

en: What happened in Ireland could happen in any Member State because there are – as I understand it – thousands of tonnes of PCBs in circulation.
reason: States a factual risk that similar incidents could happen elsewhere, without advocating any political principle or solution.

en: This accident – if that is what it was – too, must be reconstructed and it must be investigated whether this type of combustion and the smoke which it passes through the meat really can cause so much dioxin to end up in the meat.
reason: Calls for investigation of the accident’s cause; this is a technical request, not an ideological stance.

en: I fear that we will have cases like this again in future.
reason: Expresses fear of future cases; no policy recommendation or ideological content is present.

en: Even though the EU does not have any direct intervention mechanisms, Member States must be allowed to take the necessary measures to prevent the collapse of an industry on which the jobs of thousands of European citizens depend. The Romanian car industry has also been severely affected by the crisis. The serious situation at European level requires the immediate introduction of suitable measures. I am not referring, in this instance, to protectionist measures, which distort the market, but to measures which offer equal opportunities to European industry and allow employees in this industry to keep their jobs. The economic recovery plan allows this to happen because it proposes new credit regulations in the European banking system which facilitate access to credit. It is also important that the State aid schemes which Member States apply for can be accessed rapidly and easily.
reason: Advocates EU state‑aid and credit measures to protect strategic industry jobs, a clear stance on economic intervention and market regulation.

en: The European Union’s economy is reputed to be the greatest economic power in the world. One of these consequences is that it is difficult to define which car manufacturers are truly European. The mechanism for providing aid should also make use of money earmarked for targeted investment in technological innovations, in accordance with guidelines for improving road safety and environmental protection.
reason: Calls for targeted EU aid to fund technological innovation, road safety and environmental protection, expressing a pro‑environmental, innovation‑oriented policy position.

en: Such a situation justifies exceptional measures, particularly in the case of strategic sectors such as car manufacturing, which represents 6% of jobs. In reality, how can the Commission guarantee that it is out there checking coordination and that countries are not embarking on a war of support measures? What mechanisms are out there to safeguard jobs in countries that do not have the financial structure to guarantee the jobs that are vital to them? For some countries, textiles or electronics may be just as important as car making.
reason: Calls for exceptional measures to safeguard jobs in strategic sectors and questions EU coordination mechanisms, showing a clear preference for protective industrial policy.

en: The matter of the return and transfer of the Guantánamo inmates may be a sign of an important shift in US policy in the right direction, namely towards respect for fundamental rights, as well as humanitarian and international law. reason: Demands respect for fundamental rights and humanitarian protection for Guantánamo detainees, articulating a strong human‑rights and rule‑of‑law foreign‑policy stance.

en: Personally, I am grateful that the United States yet again took on a disproportionate responsibility for protecting Europe from terrorism. reason: Insists that Guantánamo inmates are the United States' responsibility and should be tried under US law, expressing a clear position on national sovereignty and jurisdiction.

en: Therefore, this seems to me to be a good opportunity to respond to the request of the USA by putting forward a common position in line with the values of the European Union.
reason: Mentions aligning with EU values in response to the USA but provides no concrete policy principle; only a vague value reference.

en: According to the Commission’s figures, between 4.5 and 8 million third-party nationals are living illegally within the European Union and are therefore the favoured targets of unscrupulous employers benefiting from illegal labour.
reason: Notes the number of illegal third‑party nationals and exploitative employers but does not explicitly advocate a policy change or principle.

en: Unfortunately this type of approach has become more common in the run-up to the European elections.
reason: Comments that a certain approach is becoming more common before elections without specifying any political principle or stance.

en: For this reason, it is imperative that environmental policy remains a top priority for the EU and individual Member States.
reason: Calls for environmental policy to remain a top EU priority, a clear ideological commitment to environmental protection.

reason: Highlights a measure to reduce Europe’s energy dependency as a priority, indicating a strong stance on energy security and strategic autonomy.

reason: Advocates specific EU climate targets, energy‑efficiency standards and leadership in international negotiations – a clear environmental‑regulation stance.

en: Just today, the European Union has granted EUR 41 million in aid to the United Nations Agency for Palestine Refugees. reason: Calls for EU financial aid to UNRWA and renewed diplomatic negotiations on the Palestinian issue, expressing a concrete foreign‑policy position.

en: You cannot rebuild homes and offices without cement and glass, which are banned. We have to put pressure on the Israeli Government to end the blockade and open the crossings. We saw schools, factories, homes and a hospital deliberately attacked.
reason: Calls for pressure on Israel to end the blockade and condemns attacks, explicitly demanding a political change in the Israeli‑Palestinian conflict.

en: I thought of some of the leaders of our Member States, of all those who will answer to history for their lack of political courage, the missed opportunities, for their lack of vision. What has Europe done to seize this opportunity?

Familiarising the population with both the benefits of integration and with the commitments which they assume once a country has joined the EU will have the effect of involving them actively in the democratisation process in society and considerably reduce the ability of the elite who are in power to use coercive measures against opposition political parties and civil society.
reason: Emphasises informing populations, democratic participation and limiting elite coercion, reflecting a strong commitment to democracy and civil‑society empowerment.

en: With regards to the use of this funding, it is particularly important to ensure the transparency of other sources, including private finance. The European Union should give more effective support to civil society and to political parties which are defending democracy.
reason: Advocates EU support for civil society and parties defending democracy – a clear stance on democratic governance and EU’s role in promoting it.

en: From the point of view of the security and welfare of our common home, both eastern and southern neighbours are equally important to us. Due to the events of the past summer – here I refer to the Russo-Georgian conflict – our eastern neighbours in my opinion justifiably expect a greater contribution from the EU to the safeguarding of stability. The EU’s involvement must not be limited just to declarative political support, but must also contain very real cooperation and assistance with the implementation of reforms. I am incredibly happy that Estonia is one of the 15 founding members of the recently founded Neighbourhood Investment Facility.
reason: Calls for stronger EU security and stability involvement in Eastern neighbours, endorsing concrete EU action and reform assistance – explicit foreign‑policy principle.

en: The crisis leads to a drop in prices for raw materials, fewer investments, less trade credit and less money being sent home by immigrants. That is why we have been looking for a modest instrument with which the EU can implement policy in developing countries that does not, strictly speaking, fall within the scope of fighting poverty. The EU’s own interests – European students making study trips – may not be financed under Article 179. Moreover, the EU, when spending development funds, has to meet the criteria legally prescribed in respect of development cooperation, namely those of fighting poverty. As rapporteur – and the Committee on Development will back me up on this – I cannot agree to Article 179 as the legal basis.
reason: Discusses legal basis for EU development funding and the need to respect poverty‑fighting criteria – a procedural argument with a weak ideological angle about aid priorities.

en: Therefore, the most realistic option seems to be the creation of a new instrument for actions other than public development aid for countries falling under the Regulation.
reason: Suggests a new instrument for non‑aid actions; primarily a technical suggestion without a broader political principle.

en: So, I welcome Commissioner Ferrero-Waldner’s statement that Article 181a is there to make it possible to look for the funds to do what some of my colleagues are hoping to do.
reason: Welcomes a statement about a legal article to enable funding; expression is limited to procedural support, not an ideological stance.

en: This separation is a very relevant political message in itself and it would give proper visibility to the EU’s development cooperation policy.
reason: Notes that separating funding streams is a political message, hinting at a preference for clearer EU development policy but lacks a concrete principle.

en: The European Union has set up numerous programmes and financial instruments under the auspices of different agencies, each covering only certain limited aspects of the problems that the developing countries are currently facing. At the moment, the European Union is both institutionally fragmented and legally hindered as far as development aid is concerned.
reason: Criticises EU fragmentation and legal hindrances in development aid, implying a belief in more integrated and effective EU institutions – moderate ideological content.

en: The Committee on Development opts for a narrow interpretation of Article 179 and must therefore resort to articles intended for domestic policies as a legal basis. The Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Committee on Legal Affairs, Parliament’s Legal Service, the ECJ, the Council and the Commission all read Article 179 differently.
reason: Describes differing legal interpretations of an article; mainly factual without advocating a political principle.

en: Financing actions of this kind is important from a political perspective as it can ensure continuity of the European Union’s presence in the countries and regions which have already gone beyond the initial development stage. However, it is vitally important that the funds used to finance these actions do not come from sources earmarked for development, but from different budget lines.
reason: Emphasises financing continuity while keeping funds separate from development budgets; a procedural view with minimal ideological implication.

en: I endorse his first comment about the economic crisis, its particular impact on the developing world and, indeed, the fact that we are not reaching our target of 0.7% in aid. The use of Article 179 as the legal basis for non-development activities is clearly not appropriate and, as such, would contravene both the EC Treaty and the acquis communautaire. It also opens the possibility that, in future, non-ODA activities may be financed from budget lines which are intended for genuine development activities.
reason: Endorses the 0.7 % aid target and argues against using Article 179 for non‑development activities, asserting adherence to treaty obligations and proper aid policy.

en: Creditworthiness is particularly important during financial crises, so that these enterprises can still obtain microcredit. It is with this in mind that I hope development policy takes the right course.
reason: The statement only expresses a vague hope that development policy will be correct; it does not explicitly advocate a concrete political principle or institutional change.

en: I am not against this if the Commission sees it as a way out for the non-ODA activities we all deem necessary and important, and I will go along with it. If I cannot reach agreement with the PPE-DE Group before we vote tomorrow at noon – which will be a pity – I shall ask for a referral back to my committee. I would be very sorry if this is the position of the PPE-DE Group, because we all agree on the need to maintain development aid at the level it is today, and we all know that it is shrinking with the economic crisis.
reason: Calls for maintaining current levels of development aid, indicating a preference for a specific funding policy, but the argument is relatively general and not strongly framed as an ideological commitment.

en: The Committee on Foreign Affairs does not consider it desirable to limit the new legal basis for the instrument to a few areas of cooperation. In addition, the policy fields currently envisaged (culture, youth, research) are borrowed from European domestic policy and have not, up to now, been intended to define cooperation with third countries. What happens, for example, if, in the near future, it becomes desirable to cooperate with other countries in matters of climate policy? Do we have to create a new legal basis for the instrument each time? This is the only reason why the Group of the Greens/European Free Alliance, together with the second rapporteur from the Committee on Foreign Affairs, withdrew the amendment on Monday. However, this report is just a recommendation to the Commission.
reason: Argues for a flexible legal basis for EU external cooperation instruments and mentions climate policy, reflecting a clear stance on how EU foreign policy should be structured.

en: To conclude, I would once again like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs, the Commission for their excellent contribution, and also the services of the ITRE Committee for the help that they have given me in drawing up this report. I must say that Parliament agrees with the Commission that, in view of the globalisation of research and the emergence of new scientific and technological powers such as China and India, we urgently need to speed up, and, to that end, incentivise, the construction of a new European research area. On this point I would like to say once again that in an initiative of this calibre, Parliament should have played a much more decisive role.
reason: Advocates speeding up and incentivising a new European research area and a more decisive parliamentary role, explicitly promoting deeper EU integration in research.

en: We are talking here not only about research carried out at universities – academic research – or in industry but also, in particular, about research carried out in small and medium-sized enterprises. After all, it is also important that these research results continue to be presented and made available. The Commission’s initiative on this is particularly to be welcomed, therefore, as the organisation of such initiatives of course reinforces the international possibilities. International cooperation, in particular, is increasingly important for us in Europe, as it is for our partners. After all, we in Europe have made ourselves the part of the world with the greatest purchasing power, and our 500 million citizens have the right to have the research results drawn up as quickly and efficiently as possible.
reason: Emphasises international research cooperation and citizens' right to rapid results, showing support for a policy of open, EU‑wide research collaboration.

en: Young, ambitious European researchers will not be forced to travel across the ocean to implement their ideas.
reason: Mentions that European researchers will not have to go abroad, a statement of preference but without a clear political principle or policy prescription.

en: I am convinced that by setting up a network of scientific research partnerships among Member States, we will be able to achieve a competitive and profitable economy based on knowledge and innovation. It would not be possible to exchange knowledge without the relevant infrastructure, because it plays a key role in establishing an effective environment for carrying out up-to-date and extremely necessary research. We also have not had the relevant legal instruments which would make it possible to set up a suitable partnership with participants from various states which is, in fact, the key to success in this area.
reason: Calls for a network of Member State research partnerships and legal instruments to build a knowledge‑based economy, clearly endorsing a specific EU‑level structural policy.

en: The truth is, of course, that institutional competition is necessary for successful institutional reforms. Imagine if an international legal research framework had been established 50 years ago. Changing international treaties is difficult and proceeds far too slowly. Progress is made if countries can easily reform their national institutions. However, the proposal is ruined completely by the fact that the Commission also wishes to regulate the taxation of this legal entity at EU level.
reason: Defends institutional competition and opposes EU‑level taxation of a legal entity, presenting a strong position on national sovereignty versus EU fiscal authority.

en: It is absurd, to say the least, to note that special permission is required from the European Union for that but still, it is progress.
reason: Criticises the need for EU permission in a vague way; no concrete political principle or policy proposal is articulated.

en: I welcome the fact that these infrastructures can receive cofinancing through Cohesion Policy financial instruments, in accordance with the regulations on the European Regional Development Fund, the Social Fund and Cohesion Fund. I want to emphasise that it is vitally important that these infrastructures establish the link between research institutes and structures, universities, academia and the private sector, with industrial sectors benefiting from the use of research results. However, I would like to mention that, above all during the current crisis, we need to make sure that at least 1% of a Member State’s GDP is allocated to research.
reason: Calls for co‑financing via cohesion funds and a specific target of 1 % of GDP for research, explicitly advocating a budgetary policy for EU research investment.

en: The notion of a common European Research Area and of a Community legal framework that is applicable to European research infrastructures has been the basic principle for achieving the objectives of the Lisbon Strategy relating to economic growth, the creation of jobs and establishing a dynamic, knowledge-based economy. We have proposed to provide research with competitive financing, adequate infrastructures and intellectual property regulations, as well as efficient mobility for researchers in our desire for the European Union to be a top international research partner. Homogenous distribution of these infrastructures and of research opportunities within the European Union would be beneficial to the whole European Union and would help to combat the migration of scientists from East to West.
reason: Advocates a common European Research Area, a Community legal framework and homogeneous distribution of research infrastructure – a clear stance on EU integration and research policy, expressing how the EU should be structured.

en: I fully support the establishment of legal status for new European research infrastructures for pan-European research projects and pan-European funding. Could you extrapolate from what we are experiencing at the moment in the EU, with what we have available in FP7 and from Member States, in view of the collapse of economic growth throughout the EU at the moment – we are not alone globally – whether we will be able to compensate with increased public sector funding in R&D? My second point concerns the frightening prospect as regards the EU’s world share in patent applications, which has declined by an alarming figure.
reason: Supports legal status for pan‑European research infrastructures and calls for increased public‑sector R&D funding, indicating a firm position on state‑driven research investment.

en: Therefore, I endorse the measures concerning the establishment of a legal framework for the European Research Infrastructure. The question of appropriate taxation is also important in this case. I also think that better cooperation is needed between research centres and the economy, including small and medium-sized enterprises. We should remember that the Lisbon Strategy provides for a share of three per cent of GDP for expenditure on research and development.
reason: Endorses a legal framework for research infrastructure, stresses appropriate taxation and a 3 % of GDP target for R&D, showing a concrete fiscal and research policy commitment.

en: The roadmap drawn up by ESFRI was certainly a step forward towards better planning of research infrastructure at European level. It is therefore essential that we mobilise sources of funding, both national and private, as far as possible, especially from industry, although as the Commissioner rightly said, this is not a very good time. I would like to ask the Council once again to listen to our message.
reason: Calls for mobilising national and private funding for research infrastructure but does not articulate a broader ideological principle; the value signal is weak.

en: The vote will take place on Thursday, 19 February 2009.
reason: Only provides the date of a vote; no political principle or ideological stance is expressed.

en: I firmly believe that by establishing this institutional framework for supporting research activity, we will see results which will bolster the European economy. The reason for this is that research is not a fad, but a necessity which guarantees the European economy's competitiveness at a global level. I would like to stress one extremely important area where research can play an important role. In the next 25 years, as a result of urbanisation, it is expected that almost 25% of land will be withdrawn from agricultural use. This is yet another reason for supporting greater research activity and ensuring a uniform European framework.
reason: Frames research as essential for European economic competitiveness and cites urbanisation impacts, advocating a strong EU‑wide research framework – a clear policy position.

en: I welcome the report on establishing a legal framework for the European Research Infrastructure (ERI), as well as the Commission’s proposal for a regulation in this area. ERI is a response to a real need on the part of European researchers and will undoubtedly help boost competitiveness in European science. Community policies in this area must combine scientific excellence with triggering an influx of researchers and effective infrastructures into countries, such as the new members of the European Union from the accession rounds in 2004 and 2007.
reason: Welcomes a legal framework and stresses the need to attract researchers to new member states, reflecting a commitment to EU enlargement and integrated research policy.

en: That is why I think it is right that we make a political commitment, at the highest level, on behalf of and with children. The EU must see in its partnership with the developing countries the opportunity to influence public policy to save children’s lives. Priority actions for children must be promoted when the European Commission negotiates the country strategy papers’ regional and thematic strategies, when they are drawn up, and subsequently when they are reviewed. I welcome the Commission’s intention to draw up partner national action plans for children. We need assurances that even the most marginalised children – including children with disabilities and orphans – have access to equitable health, welfare and judicial services. I believe there needs to be more and better training of Commission staff – both in Brussels and in delegations – particularly in how they manage the participation of children. I trust there will not be any decision that the public consultation – including with children – will be put on hold until a new Commission and Parliament is in place.
reason: Calls for a high‑level political commitment to children’s rights in EU development cooperation, demanding equitable health, welfare and judicial services – a distinct ideological stance on child welfare and EU external policy.

en: The vote will take place on Thursday, 19 February 2009.
reason: Only repeats the voting date; contains no ideological content.

en: It is our duty to ensure that we are the ones who build a better future, not only for Europeans, but also for the developing countries. It is children who represent the future and we must ensure that their rights are enforced and respected in third countries which receive European funding. It is a matter of priority that in relations with third countries, the European Union ensures that children’s rights to education and access to medical services are guaranteed. It is true that we are going through a period of financial crisis, but we cannot overlook the fact that somewhere in the world, a child dies every three seconds and every minute a woman dies in childbirth. Given that children make up half of the world's population, we must consider that the rights of children are a priority in the European Union’s development policy.
reason: Strongly emphasizes the EU’s duty to protect children’s rights in third countries receiving EU funding, linking development policy to child welfare – an explicit, robust ideological commitment.

en: The Member States must improve the implementation of the directive on informing and consulting employees, particularly in the current context of the financial crisis and of its consequences for companies as they restructure, merge or move abroad. Workers’ rights to information and consultation are essential components of the social market economy. The transposition of Directive 2002/14/EC has been considerably delayed in some Member States. In this own-initiative report, we point out that the impact of this directive is evident in the countries where no general system of worker information and consultation existed. The report also emphasises that, in their transposition measures, some Member States have not included some young workers, women working part-time or workers employed for a short period on temporary contracts. We ask that the Member States define precisely the term ‘information’ by allowing workers’ representatives to examine the data supplied and not to content themselves with awaiting the end of the information procedure if the companies’ decisions have direct consequences for the workers. Finally, in an improved coordination of the different legislative instruments, we also invite the Commission to examine what is required to coordinate the six directives and the regulation on informing employees, so that any amendments to get rid of overlaps and contradictions can be made. As this type of advance in workers’ rights is more than beneficial, the Union owes it to itself to guarantee that the Member States transpose the obligations of the directive correctly and in full.
reason: Explicitly advocates stronger EU‑wide implementation of the employee information and consultation directive, linking it to the social market economy and calling for concrete legislative coordination – a clear political principle about workers’ rights and market regulation.

en: We pass on this report, to which social actors and associations have contributed a great deal, to the Commission, in the hope that despite the short time remaining before the end of this electoral term, it will find the time, Commissioner – you represent the whole Commission here today – to put together some initiatives, and give a clear signal, so that the next Parliament and the next Commission do not have to start again from scratch but have something solid to build on. It is a sector comprised of different operators – cooperatives, mutual societies, foundations, social enterprises and associations – which share specific values and make a significant contribution to GDP. These are concepts that form part of the ideological heritage of the European Union – one need only think of Delors – since we have often acknowledged the social economy as the keystone of the European social model, but then done very little about it. The world of the social economy is, by contrast, more locally rooted, closer to the real economy and to people and therefore protected from speculation, as has proved the case.
reason: Calls for Commission action to recognise and support the social economy as a keystone of the EU social model, urging concrete policy measures – clear ideological support for a specific sector and the EU’s social‑democratic heritage.

en: We call on the Commission and Member States to develop a legal framework which will recognise the social economy as a third sector and apply regulations that clearly stipulate which entities can operate in this sector so that no other type of organisation can benefit from the funding or public policies intended to encourage enterprises in the social economy. We also call on the Commission and Member States to offer financial support, training and consultancy and also to simplify the procedures for setting up enterprises in the social sector. In this way, the social economy will fulfil its effective role against the general backdrop of the European economy, by not only helping combat poverty, but also by facilitating access to resources, rights and services which citizens need to be able to participate in society.
reason: Demands a legal framework that recognises the social economy as a third sector, with regulations, funding and simplification, showing a firm stance on how the EU economy should be structured.

en: Social economy indeed requires visibility – through better knowledge of EU-wide data – for better achieving the objectives of solidarity, employment, entrepreneurship, growth, competitiveness social cohesion and social dialogue in the Union as a whole. Social economy is increasingly becoming an important actor at local and regional levels and has now, more than ever – due to the serious impacts of the financial crisis – a major role to play in European social and economic development.
reason: Emphasises the need for data visibility to achieve solidarity, employment and cohesion goals of the social economy, indicating a supportive but less concrete ideological position.

en: We have talked and written a lot about the social economy, but without a European statistical base it will not become visible in our everyday lives. Participating organisations, on the other hand, are too small to become known on a macro-economic level.
reason: Only notes the lack of a statistical base for the social economy without proposing any policy change; essentially a factual observation, not a clear ideological commitment.

en: Depression is one of the most common disorders and, by 2020, will be the most common illness in the developed world. We will therefore all agree that there is a need to take a concerted approach to the challenges posed by mental health and that it concerns us all. At the same time, we are formulating proposals within the framework of the five priority areas of the Pact.
reason: Mentions the widespread nature of depression and a need for a concerted approach within the Pact, but offers no specific policy prescription – weak value signal.

en: Mental health disorders are national health problems in many countries, as they have a significant influence on the people involved, their families and society in general. Mental health disorders also often lead to disability and can thus cause a significant economic burden on society. In accordance with the World Bank’s 1993 development report, four of the ten most common causes of disability were mental health and/or neurological disorders. Despite the extent and seriousness of the consequences of mental health disorders, there are still countries in the world and in Europe today where insufficient attention is devoted to the problem. This, in turn, leads to insufficient attention being devoted to mental health, limited availability of services, the shortage of alternative treatment methods and insufficient information about treatment possibilities.
reason: Highlights insufficient attention to mental health and its societal costs, implicitly calling for more focus, yet without concrete political proposals – a vague ideological cue.

en: I think that we should take far-reaching steps to defeat these diseases of civilisation. Such people very often display antipathy towards others, feel alienated, and have a fear of the censure of society.
reason: General call for ‘far‑reaching steps’ against disease without specifying political measures; lacks clear ideological content.

en: Parliament’s initiative to improve information on mental health is a very positive step, therefore. There should be more public discussion of approaches to mental disorders and, in addition, methods for preventing mental illness should be made accessible to the general public.
reason: Praises a parliamentary initiative and urges more public discussion and accessibility of prevention methods for mental illness – modest advocacy for public policy awareness.

en: Likewise, here in the European Parliament, there has been a lot of discussion about various alternative transportation routes, the expansion of storage capacities, as well as the future role of nuclear energy. I am particularly pleased that the report on the National Energy Efficiency Action Plans has provided an opportunity to discuss this topic during the last few weeks. The significance of energy efficiency lies in its ability to achieve perceptible results faster than by any other means. As Energy Commissioner Andris Piebalgs has recently pointed out, EU measures on off mode devices could reduce standby losses by the equivalent of Hungary’s annual energy consumption. Therefore, we agree with the 2006 EU Directive setting out measures for the Member States to summarise in National Action Plans their planned measures for improving energy efficiency. In the current report, we attempted to draw general conclusions regarding the aforementioned Action Plans. At the same time, our goal was to define necessary future steps in EU legislation. Secondly, resources dedicated to improving energy efficiency need to be increased at both national and Community levels. Thirdly, there is a continued need for legislation in energy efficiency in the European Union.
reason: Strongly supports EU energy‑efficiency legislation, calls for increased resources and further legal measures, reflecting a clear environmental‑policy stance.

en: Therefore, let me remind you that it is important to diversify EU energy sources and supply routes more with the aim of mitigating the negative effects which may arise due to a future oil crisis. The dependency of EU Member States, in particular EU ‘energy islands’, on the import of energy supplies and existing infrastructure varies. Can we talk of a single energy market, if, for example, the Baltic States, including Lithuania, are energy islands? On paper, we are creating an ambitious European energy policy but, in practice, the bilateral energy policy continues to dominate. We could and should try to change the situation through diversification and solidarity. We must complete the missing energy links and establish an EU coordinating mechanism, aimed at reacting to similar crises. It is essential that Member States which are most dependent on energy supplies have sufficient reserves of these supplies.
reason: Explicitly advocates EU‑wide diversification of energy sources, a coordinating mechanism and solidarity, outlining how EU energy policy should be structured.

en: Experience from the first assessment of the national action plans demonstrates in practice that conditions in the EU have not yet matured to the point at which measures to promote energy efficiency can be supported. The EU should therefore proceed without further delay to include energy efficiency in all its sectoral policies, with clear proposals and support measures, and to increase Community aid in this direction.
reason: Calls for the EU to embed energy efficiency in all sectoral policies and increase Community aid, clearly stating a policy position for EU governance.

en: Greater investment in research and development, and in the collection and processing of reliable data, would result in a more solid and sustainable Common Fisheries Policy. Firstly, Commissioner, the amounts laid down in the Seventh Framework Programme for marine research, which should have been a cross-cutting issue, seem to be insufficient for the integrated approach that is currently desired for this issue. To summarise, the objective of European Union maritime policy of achieving productive fisheries in a clean marine environment requires that the scientists that work in this field have access to horizontal funding mechanisms in the Seventh Framework Programme.
reason: Demands greater EU investment in R&D and funding mechanisms for a sustainable Common Fisheries Policy, indicating a concrete stance on EU budgetary priorities.

en: For this reason, apart from Member States’ efforts to become actively involved in promoting policies aimed at making energy consumption more efficient, there must also be coordination at Community level in order to achieve much better results. According to a study, it is possible at Community level to reduce energy loss by roughly 27%, which means, by implication, a reduction in the costs which citizens are obliged to pay. As a result, the measures which will be taken in the future must consider simplifying these procedures.
reason: Calls for Community‑level coordination on energy‑efficiency measures and procedural simplification, expressing a clear preference for EU‑wide regulatory action.

en: Energy efficiency is all the more important at the moment as we face real challenges concerning the provision of energy supplies to the EU and as we need to make more consistent efforts to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. I support an approach to the energy efficiency problem which is consistent with the other EU policies, in particular, the package for combating climate change and the necessity to diversify energy sources. I firmly believe that the R&D sector must be supported as this can make a significant contribution to boosting energy efficiency. The Commission and Member State governments should give stronger support to projects intended to boost energy efficiency, whether we are talking about investments to make public transport as energy efficient as possible, insulating buildings, etc. I think that government resources should be channelled more in this direction rather than towards subsidising the price of energy, as these projects provide, at the same time, support to vulnerable consumers faced with rising energy prices.
reason: Supports a policy mix that prioritises R&D and government funding for energy‑efficiency over price subsidies, showing a distinct ideological view on resource allocation.

en: One in four people suffer from mental health problems at least once in their life. It is estimated that by the year 2020, depression will have become the most common illness in the developed world and the second main reason for incapacity for work. Although there have been dramatic leaps forward as regards standards of care and general attitude, people who suffer from mental health problems and their families are being marginalised more and more often.
reason: Only describes mental‑health prevalence and marginalisation without proposing any policy or ideological stance.

en: I support this report since it entails a comprehensive approach to the challenges we face in the mental health sector, such as combating stigma, discrimination and social exclusion, but also recognising the need for preventive programs, public support and adequate treatment of people. I believe we should strongly support further research in this area, with special attention to the growing elderly population in Europe, which is hoping for a healthy, dignified and active ageing.
reason: Advocates stronger public support, research and preventive programmes for mental health, but the stance is general and not tied to a specific political principle.

en: I feel that the European Union and Member States should encourage and support forms of implementation of the social economy, e.g. cooperatives, mutual societies, associations and foundations, in their legislation and policies. I feel that the role of women in the social economy must be reinforced, given their involvement in associations and voluntary organisations. I urge the Commission to integrate the social economy in the other policies and strategies for social and economic development, especially in light of the Small Business Act, as the structures of the social economy are primarily targeted at small and medium-sized enterprises and services of general interest. These efforts could also be supported by creating a statistical register of enterprises in the social economy in each European Union Member State and by inputting the data into the EUROSTAT European statistics system.
reason: Strongly promotes the social economy, gender inclusion, and integration of these sectors into EU policies, reflecting a clear ideological commitment to social‑economy and gender equity.

en: I also feel that it must become an obligatory practice in the situation where a multinational company is being restructured for trade-union representatives from all branches of the company to be invited to negotiations and consulted, not only those from the Member State in which the company has its head office. I feel that it is important to regularly update the legislation concerning the rights of workers to be informed and consulted and include this item on the agenda for European social dialogue, both at an interprofessional and industrial level.
reason: Calls for mandatory EU‑wide trade‑union representation in multinational restructurings and updated workers’ rights legislation, a firm position on labour rights and EU governance.

en: I have taken a particular interest in the issue of children’s rights in the context of foreign relations. My opinion stresses that all measures in the interests of children’s rights should give priority status to parents and immediate relatives of children. The opinion asks the Commission to emphasise the importance of the need to register every child at birth in all third countries as part of the Commission’s development policy, and to make its aid programmes dependent on this requirement. I support any attempt to promote development aid. I do, however, insist that humanitarian organisations and international bodies responsible for allocating aid guarantee that the aid and funding allocated actually reaches the children it is destined for, and is not squandered.
reason: Advocates linking development aid to child‑registration requirements and stresses children’s rights in foreign policy, indicating a concrete policy principle for EU external action.

en: It is tragic that many lives can be saved with the appropriate measures, be they medical or financial, and still the situation is aggravating. Special attention has to be given to the most vulnerable and socially excluded girls and boys, including disabled children, migrant children and children from minorities. The Committee on Development adopted this own-initiative report (drafted by Glenys Kinnock (PES, UK) on a special place of children in EU external action in response to the Commission communication on the subject.
reason: Advocates a concrete policy of giving special attention to vulnerable and migrant children, expressing a clear stance on social protection and inclusion within EU external action.

en: Establishing European research infrastructures guarantees that research will reach a high level. In addition, it will create new opportunities for closer collaboration between teams of European researchers which may also be joined by numerous students and technical staff, thereby helping attract young people into hi-tech research. This legal framework must also ensure better cooperation between industry and academic research, thereby facilitating the implementation of innovations. I support the rapporteur’s proposal which asks the Commission to regularly report to the European Parliament on the status regarding the development of the European research infrastructures. Establishing a common legal framework is absolutely necessary in order to facilitate and accelerate the development of these infrastructures.
reason: Calls for a common legal framework and EU investment in research infrastructures, clearly supporting EU‑wide scientific collaboration and market regulation in research.

en: A little over a year ago, on 8 January 2008, you received a communication from the Deputy Secretary-General, on a decision of the Conference of Presidents of 27 October 2007. Point 3(B) very clearly states that ‘catch the eye’ time is a maximum of five minutes, and is limited to a maximum of one minute per speaker.
reason: Only describes procedural rules for speaking time; no political principle or ideological position is advanced.

en: The Union’s central role as a key actor in development cooperation should be strengthened even further in the future. In order to stabilise the economies of the developing countries and bring peace to them, it is vitally important that the Union keeps to its target to increase its share of development aid by 0.7% of GDP by the year 2015. This alone, however, will not be enough. It is essential to achieve general coherence in development cooperation among the different institutions. Financial investment and projects intended to build infrastructure and for more satisfactory adherence to the notion of human rights need to be undertaken in such a way that they support one another. The EU needs to establish the necessary instruments for implementing coherent development policy measures. The Union’s current legal basis for development cooperation, however, is flawed in terms of legislation, and that is why I would like to thank the rapporteur for raising what is an important issue. Projects aimed at improving the transport, technology and energy sectors and the dialogue between the scientific community and NGOs are essential for the social viability of developing countries. reason: Opposes a European private‑company statute and urges Parliament to signal rejection, reflecting a clear preference for national over EU‑wide company law.

en: They are included in full in the amendments that we have adopted and I believe that, with these amendments, it is wholly admissible to adopt the text, even from Mr Wurtz’s viewpoint.
reason: Mentions procedural adoption of amendments without expressing any substantive political principle.

reason: Advocates a specific policy principle: prioritize SMEs in public tenders and prevent public authorities from intervening in competition, indicating a clear market‑regulation stance.

During these difficult times, we have to do everything we possibly can to make sure that businesses survive until the hoped-for upturn. If we want to get our small businesses and employment to stabilise in the European Union and in each individual Member State, we must do everything we possibly can to try and save them.

In conclusion, I would like to say that it is particularly important to allocate EUR 30 000 million in the 2009-2011 period to encourage lending to SMEs.

en: We assert that they are essential to the health of the European economy.
reason: Simply asserts that SMEs are essential to the economy; this is generic praise without a specific ideological stance.
