reason: Advocates maintaining a 500‑employee threshold to avoid additional costs for smaller firms, reflecting a concrete regulatory preference.

en: Administrative bodies should adjust to their needs and family orientation in order to facilitate their existence, their transfer, particularly in cases of illness, retirement or bankruptcy, and their winding-up. The 23 million European SMEs cannot be subject to the same requirements as the 41 000 large undertakings. Moves in this direction include the European private company statute, the initiatives to create companies in 48 hours, to reduce administrative costs by 25% by 2012, the creation of a one-stop scheme for VAT and reduced VAT rates for labour-intensive and locally supplied services, and a common consolidated corporate tax base. SMEs should increase their participation in the internal market and in public procurement. Ways to promote more balanced competition conditions would be to facilitate the exemption from new State aid categories, to promote cooperation, to amend the directive on late payment in order to ensure payment within 30 days, and to remove obstacles to public procurement.
reason: Provides a detailed set of policy proposals (tax base, one‑stop VAT, reduced admin costs, procurement rules) aimed at reshaping competition in favor of SMEs, indicating strong ideological commitment.

en: Small and medium-sized enterprises have a totally different capacity from traditional large enterprises when it comes to adapting to new circumstances and adopting new discoveries and technology. In addition to making it easier for small businesses to participate in public procurement by providing better access to the internal market, making it easier to obtain capital and making the rules on state aid non-discriminatory, there must also be a change in attitude permeating all decision-making, in schools, universities and the workplace. Research shows that there is a strong correlation between entrepreneurship and growth. The forthcoming Swedish Presidency will, in particular, be making targeted efforts to facilitate enterprise by women, an important European strategy for the future.
reason: Outlines a comprehensive agenda to facilitate SME participation, gender‑focused entrepreneurship, and EU‑wide market access, showing a clear pro‑SME, pro‑EU integration stance.

reason: Proposes a new standardized European company form with minimal bureaucracy, a specific institutional reform that reflects a clear regulatory principle.

reason: Explicitly supports a directive for reduced VAT rates on labour‑intensive, locally supplied services, showing a clear fiscal‑policy stance.

Member States must therefore carefully review their legal and fiscal framework to improve the conditions for the transfer of businesses and to promote and apply effective models for the transfer of businesses to employees as an alternative to their closure. This approach would allow jobs to be protected and profits to be reinvested in order to better develop these businesses. To end, I would point out that support for innovative projects of small and medium-sized enterprises, easier access to European funds and improved access to credit, particularly, but not only, in the current context, are vital factors for supporting SMEs.
reason: Advocates reforms to legal and fiscal frameworks, employee ownership, and increased EU funding for SMEs, indicating a defined economic‑policy position.

reason: Calls for maximum EU funding sources and credit mechanisms for SMEs, expressing a clear policy preference for financial support of small businesses.

reason: Advocates a special SME fund, micro‑credits, and legal recognition of co‑ownership for women, combining economic support with gender‑equality principles.

en: We are at present in a paradoxical situation whereby recognition rates of candidates to refugee status for certain third country nationals vary from approximately 0% up to 90% depending on which Member State receives the request. We must ensure that international conventions are correctly applied, as well as cooperation agreements with third countries. Member States cannot detain people for the sole reason that they are applying for international protection.
reason: Denounces inconsistent refugee‑status decisions and detention of asylum seekers, emphasizing adherence to international conventions and protection rights.

en: In recent years, the number of refugees worldwide has reached 16 million. In 2007, the EU received more than 200 000 asylum applications. I would also like to draw attention to the fact that the European Commission’s Policy Plan on Asylum does not mention the Frontex agency, which plays a very important role in the area of refugee protection. Moreover, it is important to mention that the number of asylum applicants depends directly on the political, economic and social situation in the countries of origin of the asylum applicants.
reason: Notes shortcomings in the EU asylum policy and links refugee flows to origin-country conditions, offering a weak but present critique of current policy.

en: In 2008, as already highlighted by the rapporteur, the number of refugees grew to over 12 million. We therefore urgently need to begin the second phase of the Common European Asylum System. Only in this way can asylum seekers be treated equally, regardless of the Member State in which they make their asylum application.
reason: Advocates a second phase of the Common European Asylum System to ensure equal treatment of asylum seekers across Member States – a clear stance on EU integration and solidarity.

en: Besides the single common procedure and content of protection, there needs to be practical cooperation, support and solidarity, including through the important European Asylum Support Office, providing common sources of country information.
reason: Calls for a single common procedure, cooperation, support and solidarity via the European Asylum Support Office – explicit endorsement of coordinated EU asylum policy.

en: In summary, our EU procedures should be unified, transparent and fast.
reason: States that EU asylum procedures should be unified, transparent and fast – clear policy prescription reflecting a pro‑EU regulatory position.

en: We should not be trying to create new EU standards, which, with all probability, would be more restrictive than the Geneva Convention, for example.
reason: Opposes creation of new EU standards that would be more restrictive than the Geneva Convention – a definitive opposition to stricter asylum rules.

en: As a result of the major discrepancies in the decision-making processes which the 27 Member States use for dealing with asylum applications, the rate in terms of acknowledging applicants’ refugee status varies between 0% and approximately 90%. In addition, the Dublin system’s criteria place a disproportionate burden on Member States located at the European Union’s external border as they are responsible for processing asylum applications as the first country of entry. However, the most difficult problem to resolve remains communication between Member States about the different treatment given to applicants for international protection according to their country of origin. I hope that the regulation for creating a European Asylum Support Office, proposed by the Commission three weeks ago, will help partially resolve the current issues.
reason: Highlights uneven burden among Member States and supports a regulation for a European Asylum Support Office, indicating a solidarity‑based stance though expressed with some hopeful language.

en: I fully share the view that it is unfortunate that entry into force has been postponed until 2012. I think that it is good that Parliament is calling attention to the fact that children and minors should receive special support. For what crimes other than people trafficking is cooperation a requirement for asylum? The third issue is how different countries receive asylum seekers and which countries are chosen.
reason: Expresses agreement with delaying implementation and emphasizes special support for children, but mixes personal opinions and questions, resulting in a weaker ideological signal.

en: As the report states, there are currently about 12 million refugees and about 26 million internally displaced persons worldwide. The report proposes a common European asylum system and a common asylum support office with common standards for granting refugee and asylum status. Many, if not most, of those people who seek refugee and asylum status in European countries far from home are, of course, economic migrants seeking a better life.
reason: Describes the need for a common European asylum system and support office while noting many applicants are economic migrants – shows a clear policy preference for EU‑wide coordination.

en: This clause is applied on a voluntary basis and allows migrants that arrive in one country seeking asylum to be able to transfer to another European Union country. This Parliament even allocated EUR 5 million in this year’s European Union budget so as to facilitate the implementation of this clause.
reason: Provides factual description of a voluntary clause and budget allocation without explicit normative judgement; only a faint policy implication.

en: In this respect, I welcome the proposal to create a European Asylum Support Office to coordinate the various countries’ national policies in order to avoid a disproportionate burden being imposed on certain Member States.
reason: Welcomes the creation of a European Asylum Support Office to avoid disproportionate burdens – explicit endorsement of solidarity and EU‑level coordination.

en: We do recognise the need for solidarity, but I think that those who have already had to suffer so much in life should not be punished once again with a harsh climate unless they choose it themselves. If we have a common border, it is logical that asylum seekers should receive equal treatment throughout the European Union.
reason: Affirms the need for solidarity and equal treatment of asylum seekers across the EU, rejecting harsher measures – strong ideological commitment to equality and shared responsibility.

en: We need to act jointly and more firmly to combat illegal economic migration, while providing more dignified conditions to asylum seekers. It troubles me that the children of refugees in European camps have no access to education or necessary health care for months at a time.
reason: Explicitly advocates a joint EU stance to curb illegal economic migration while improving asylum seekers’ conditions, showing a clear migration policy position.

en: A unified procedure should be established for granting asylum, as well as unified standards which enable decisions to be made about who should be recognised as a refugee or whether a person is in need of international protection. During the waiting period, it is extremely important for the authorities to give due consideration to the diverse needs of asylum seekers in more difficult circumstances, such as children, disabled people and women. It is worth emphasising that the obligation to provide assistance is guaranteed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and is legally binding for all EU Member States and on EU’s Frontex agency.
reason: Calls for a unified EU asylum procedure and binding legal standards, reflecting a strong stance on asylum policy and EU integration.

en: Tens of thousands of Roma children still grow up in segregated schools, where they cannot gain competitive knowledge, and they carry with them throughout their lives the wounds of exclusion and discrimination. reason: Denounces Roma segregation and argues for education, employment and reduced social assistance, revealing a clear commitment to social equality and integration.

reason: Suggests a common EU action plan with sanctions but lacks a specific principle; the statement is vague about the underlying ideological goal.

reason: Self‑identifies as “representative of the right” and promotes Roma integration based on economic contribution and labour‑market participation, a clear right‑leaning integration stance.

en: We need concrete, decisive steps in the areas of education and job creation.
reason: General call for steps in education and job creation without specifying a political principle; only a weak value signal.

reason: Criticises emergency legislative measures for Roma issues but does not propose a concrete principle; merely a complaint.

en: We have known for years that the Commission cannot always approach such controls in the Member States as it would perhaps like and as dictated by the budgetary principles and the ideas of the ECA. Therefore, our report – which was also adopted unanimously by the Committee on Budgetary Control – calls for continuous pressure to be exerted on the Member States to provide data that is both complete and comprehensible. It is my fervent hope that the Commission will continue to take seriously its task of introducing the internal control framework in future.
reason: Advocates stronger EU budgetary oversight and data transparency, indicating a moderate commitment to accountability and EU governance.

en: A study from Sweden and other countries shows that the risk of someone developing an addiction to gambling is five to seven times higher if that person plays poker on the Internet than if he or she simply goes out and plays poker in the real world.
reason: Provides a statistical finding on gambling addiction; contains no political principle or ideological stance.

I would also like to thank my colleagues from the Committee on Agriculture and Rural Development and, especially, the experts for the support they have given in promoting this report. Simplification of marketing standards, keeping consumers better informed, particularly about the origin of food products, and better protection for European quality products at a global level are some of the most important proposals in the report. reason: Pushes for consumer‑protection measures, simplified marketing standards and protection of European quality products, showing a clear policy position on market regulation.

reason: Advocates a specific EU policy – mandatory labeling of the origin of main ingredients for protected products – indicating a clear stance on market transparency and consumer information regulation.

reason: Supports the EU quality‑labelling system and stresses the importance of indicating country of origin, showing a moderate commitment to consumer‑information policy, though without proposing new measures.

reason: Strongly endorses clean technologies, renewable energy, biofuels, and energy efficiency as solutions for reducing oil dependency, cutting emissions, creating jobs and stimulating growth – a clear, explicit ideological commitment to a green‑economy agenda.

reason: Calls for greater consumer awareness of EU food standards, faster registration of regional products and promotion of EU quality symbols – a clear demand for more efficient consumer‑protection regulation.

reason: Calls for transparency, strict internal controls, avoidance of wasteful spending and simplification of EU bureaucracy – a clear stance on fiscal responsibility and efficient governance.

reason: Advocates the involvement of NGOs and Roma communities in drafting and implementing social‑inclusion policies, expressing a principle of participatory policy making for minorities.

reason: Frames Roma integration as a European problem requiring EU‑level support in social and labour‑market domains, indicating a commitment to EU solidarity and minority integration.

reason: The speaker explicitly opposes weakening a Commission proposal, supports stronger road‑safety and environmental measures, and frames this as a principled stance on public safety and climate policy.

en: The amendments discussed by all the groups to permit stricter controls on furan and dioxin emissions are also justified.

en: The European Union has been tackling this kind of environmental pollution for decades, and recently all the attention in the environmental field has been focused on CO and climate change. We in the Committee on the Environment, Public Health and Food Safety have considered the proposals in detail and have reached an acceptable compromise on many points. For example, the emission standards for power stations must be comparable to those for waste incineration plants in terms of stringency, particularly if we consider that power stations are co-incinerators of waste.
reason: Advocates strong emission standards for power stations and aligns them with waste‑incineration rules, reflecting a firm environmental protection stance.

en: For me, cutting bureaucracy does not mean the creation of new reporting obligations and complicated procedures but rather, above all, the avoidance of duplicated regulation and unnecessary burdens. By setting emissions limits that the Member States must adhere to as an absolute upper limit when granting permits to large industrial plants, we will be putting a stop to the inflationary use of derogations that has thus far taken place in certain Member States. In that way, we will be guaranteeing a uniform high level of safety. Member States will then no longer be able to gain a competitive advantage at the expense of the environment.
reason: Calls for reducing bureaucratic duplication and imposing uniform safety limits to prevent competitive advantage through weaker environmental rules, a clear principle of regulatory harmonisation and fairness.

en: However, it is also important not to permit additional derogations or longer time limits in this directive so that we are able to continue this positive development of less fallout of hazardous emissions over Europe. reason: Supports a uniform EU‑wide safety net and urges impact assessments, reflecting a clear pro‑integration, social‑policy position.

reason: Calls for a CO emission ceiling for coal plants and argues for sector‑specific regulation, indicating a definite climate‑policy stance.

en: I think there is a balance to strike between environmental protection, on the one hand, and on bureaucracy and cost to industry and smaller installations, such as farmers and healthcare installations, on the other. reason: Notes proportionality of economic impact to environmental benefits and thanks a colleague, but lacks a definitive political principle.

en: I welcome both the integrated approach (the consolidation in a single text of seven separate directives on industrial emissions) and more stringent provisions governing the use of best available techniques aimed at finding innovative solutions for reducing the pollutant effect of production. reason: Expresses support for an integrated, stricter environmental directive and the use of best‑available techniques – a clear environmental regulatory position.

en: While industrial activity has a fundamental role to play in maintaining and increasing economic well-being, we must not lose sight of the impact it has on the environment. reason: Supports a specific CO₂ emission limit for large power plants and links it to combating global warming – explicit climate‑policy stance.

en: The decision about integrated pollution prevention and control (IPPC) represents an opportunity for Europe to obtain uniformly high standards of protection. reason: Calls for uniformly high environmental protection standards and incentives for clean technology while warning against excessive bureaucracy – clear environmental regulation viewpoint.

en: The amendments by Mr Nassauer may bring some reassurances to his group and other MEPs who are concerned that some private information may get into the public domain. Some Members have raised doubts about whether all the amendments that my report proposes are within the scope of the legal basis of the regulation – Article 255 of the Treaty. reason: Defends transparency and proper legal basis for document classification, emphasizing the need for public access – a defined commitment to transparency and rule of law.

en: So, the outcome, whether through the use of this procedure or through the practical proposals that have been made, is surely a step backwards compared with the current situation.

reason: Advocates increased transparency, legal certainty, and democratic oversight in EU decision‑making – a strong commitment to democratic transparency.

reason: Explicitly advocates for citizens' right to information and greater transparency in EU legislative processes, a clear political principle.

en: An increasing amount of national legislation, with the principle of public access we have in Sweden, for example, is now being made at EU level. The Confederal Group of the European United Left/Nordic Green Left and I have submitted amendments to, among other things, broaden the definition of documents, make more documents accessible to the public and prevent any individual Member State from being able to submit a veto. Commissioner Wallström said that a good tool can always be improved.
reason: Calls for broader public access to EU documents, limits on member‑state vetoes, and links transparency to low voter turnout – a strong ideological stance on openness.

reason: Only describes existing transparency without advocating or opposing any principle; essentially a factual statement.

reason: Calls for increased public access, an open EU with no hidden agendas, and urges unified parliamentary action – clear commitment to transparency.

en: This will enable citizens to truly participate in the political process and to ask the public authorities for clarification. reason: Advocates that easy citizen access to documents is foundational for participation and rights protection, a strong democratic‑transparency position.

reason: Notes procedural flexibility and possible reluctance but does not clearly advocate a principle; only a weak value signal.

reason: Advocates increased transparency and participatory democracy in the EU by demanding publication of influencing documents, a clear political principle about how EU institutions should operate.

en: This meant the elimination of the leaders and elites of a nation fighting for its own, and Europe’s, freedom. Therefore, I will not ask for this today and will free the presidency from what appears to be such a difficult decision.

en: Whilst you might well be wanting us to vote, we have a small problem with this, because we do not know what we are voting on and we do not know which way we should be voting.
reason: Expresses confusion over voting information, a complaint about procedural clarity rather than a defined ideological position.

en: We now have Amendments 106, 139, 88 and 89.
reason: Purely factual statement listing amendment numbers; contains no political principle or value judgment.

reason: A procedural request to support an oral amendment without specifying any underlying policy principle or ideological commitment.

reason: Explicitly argues that regulatory responsibility should lie with national governments and criticises EU‑wide regulations that favour imports over domestic standards, showing a clear stance on national sovereignty versus EU integration.

reason: Only comments on procedural aspects of a parliamentary proposal without advocating any political principle or policy direction.

reason: Advocates a Europe‑wide ban on gambling advertisements targeting youth and tighter payment regulations, reflecting a strong policy stance on consumer protection and public‑health regulation.

reason: Supports voting in favour of measures that discard state‑aid rules and keep non‑viable companies alive, expressing a market‑oriented, limited‑state‑intervention ideology.

reason: Advocates specific economic policy for small businesses (credit, training, research) and stresses cross‑border EU trade, showing a clear stance on market support and integration.

reason: Demands that Romania be fully included in all EU agreements, asserting the principle of equal rights and obligations for all member states.

reason: Provides detailed recommendations for integrated border‑management tools and terminology, showing a strong ideological commitment to efficient EU border policy.

reason: Highlights insufficient attention to external‑border security, signalling a principle that security should be prioritized.

reason: Welcomes specific border‑control programmes but stresses the need for a coordinated master plan, indicating a clear policy stance on EU border strategy.

en: Finally, in the name of both solidarity and equitable justice, it must be stressed that there is a need for consideration to be given to the burden that managing external borders represents to the Member States in question.
reason: Frames border‑management burden in terms of solidarity and equitable justice, expressing a principle of fair burden‑sharing among member states.

en: Increasing border security, which should proceed in tandem with improving the free movement of people in an increasingly unified Europe, is an important element in this. reason: Critiques the EU’s neoliberal agenda, links free movement of capital/persons to political outcomes, and argues for prioritising peace and social policy – a strong ideological critique of economic liberalism.

en: I believe that a harmonised asylum system will undermine the UK’s sovereign right to decide for itself who should and should not be allowed to claim asylum in my country. reason: Opposes a harmonised asylum system on grounds of national sovereignty and ministerial accountability, explicitly advocating for UK control over asylum policy.

reason: Strongly supports a common asylum system with uniform time limits and revised Dublin rules, advocating specific EU‑wide policy reforms.

en: My party, the Dutch Socialist Party, does not believe that harmonising asylum policy and dressing up an agency to govern this in future would lead to a more even distribution of the number of asylum applications among the various Member States. en: I do not think it is my place as an MEP to tell those involved in the performing arts how they should regulate their own affairs. In fact, I think it is my job to ensure that performing artists and organisations that facilitate performing arts are as free as possible from well-meaning, but misplaced and naïve, initiatives like this one.
reason: Explicitly opposes regulatory interference in the performing arts and calls for maximal freedom, reflecting a deregulation/libertarian principle.

en: In today’s civilised world, the disparity between men and women, and majorities and minorities, must be done away with. The European Parliament must observe its past legislation and uphold the values of universal solidarity. In order to find true talent, the most capable performers and deserving applicants, women must be given equal status with men in the same fields. Depriving a group on the basis of sex or any other characteristic will not be tolerated by the EU, and it is our duty to ensure this applies across the field of the performing arts (and others areas as well). For this reason, it is my duty and that of the PPE-DE Party to give a vote of confidence to any legislation that supports equality, corrects wrongdoings, and better preserves cohesion between members of the opposite sex.
reason: Strongly advocates gender equality legislation and condemns discrimination, showing a clear feminist, egalitarian ideological commitment.

en: As far as tyres are concerned, I believe the efforts to reduce CO emissions through the use of better tyres with less rolling resistance, as well as the introduction of electronic tyre pressure monitoring systems, to be worthwhile. I am also pleased that existing stocks will not – as originally planned – have to be taken off the market within 12 months, but instead only 30 months after the introduction of a new standard.
reason: Expresses support for tyre‑related CO₂ reduction measures, indicating a pro‑environmental regulatory stance, but without a strongly articulated principle.

en: Any citizen on the planet who is aware of the magnitude assumed by global warming can act to halt the progress of this process endangering Earth.
reason: General call for citizens to act against global warming; lacks specific policy or ideological articulation.

en: This proposal for a directive seeks to revise and bring together, in a single text, seven separate directives on industrial emissions.
reason: Describes a legislative proposal without expressing any evaluative or normative position.

en: The proposal for a directive by the European Commission on industrial emissions and the amendments by the European Parliament reveal, once again, that the real objective of the ‘green economy’ is not to protect the environment, but to safeguard the profits of capital.
reason: Criticises the ‘green economy’ as a tool for protecting capital profits, signalling a pro‑market, anti‑environmental‑regulation stance.

en: − This afternoon, we voted on the Statute for a European private company. Firstly, I take the view that this proposal increases the legal uncertainty in the European Union. The relationship between the national private company and the European private company, between the applicable national law and the text of the regulation, is not made sufficiently clear. No satisfactory answers are provided to such questions. I actually think this a much better idea than the European private company. If the Commission were to endeavour to facilitate the cross-border transfer of company registered offices, reducing red tape, the whole proposal for the European private company would be redundant.
reason: Argues that the European private‑company proposal creates legal uncertainty and advocates reducing red tape, reflecting a deregulation principle.

en: With the creation of this statute, another step is taken towards the lifting of these obstacles, especially in a sector that is fundamental to the European economy. The time and money saved by SMEs through this measure, resulting from the Small Business Act, point out a clear course for future European business policy. For these reasons, Members representing the Portuguese Social Democratic Party are supporting the report.
reason: Supports a statute that eases burdens for SMEs and aligns with a business‑friendly, pro‑SME policy orientation.

en: Worker participation is a cornerstone of a democratic and social Europe. For that reason, the right to information, consultation and worker participation, without restrictions, must take the same form as in the existing rules on the European company (Societas Europae – SE) and the European cooperative society (Societas Cooperativa Europaea – SCE).
reason: Calls for unrestricted worker participation rights as a cornerstone of a democratic and social Europe, demonstrating a clear social‑democratic ideology.

en: For too long now, national monopolies controlled by governments have prevented new entrants from offering gaming services in Europe. Online gambling offers a new way for consumers to enjoy their gaming experience. It is also important in my view to take all reasonable steps to prohibit minors from gaming online.
reason: Advocates opening the gambling market by ending national monopolies (market liberalisation) while also calling for consumer protection of minors – a clear political principle about market regulation.

en: I share concerns about citizens being ripped off and the worries about gambling addiction, but note that gambling is controlled in the majority of Member States in order to protect citizens against gambling addiction and fraud and to prevent money laundering. I believe that the alternative resolution would have addressed those concerns more effectively.
reason: Mentions concerns about gambling harms and existing controls but does not explicitly advocate a specific policy direction; only a vague acknowledgment of regulation.

en: The Schaldemose report on the integrity of online gambling sets out Member States’ responsibilities in regulating their gambling markets so as to protect vulnerable consumers, especially children, to tackle crime and to protect sporting events from risks such as match-fixing. The report also makes clear that such regulation must be proportionate and non-discriminatory, as set out in the EU Treaties. A number of Member States are currently reviewing their legislation on gambling to ensure it is compliant with the EU Treaties. Labour MEPs emphasise that authorities across the EU must remain vigilant and cooperate against all risks of crime, match-fixing, and threats to young people and the vulnerable from all forms of gambling.
reason: Calls for EU Member States to regulate gambling to protect vulnerable groups and combat crime, emphasizing proportionality and non‑discrimination – a clear stance on consumer protection and rule‑of‑law principles.

en: In its case law, the European Court of Justice has confirmed that it is Member States themselves who determine what level of protection they consider appropriate to protect their citizens against the hazards associated with gambling. The subsidiarity applicable here means that Member States must be able to control and to regulate their gambling markets in accordance with their traditions and cultures in order to protect consumers against the hazards of addiction, fraud and money laundering. In view of the additional risks involved in online gambling, I am convinced that national legislation cannot be replaced by pan-European self-regulation of the gambling industry. Therefore, I join the substantial majority of my colleagues on the Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection who believe that a purely internal market approach to gambling is not applicable.
reason: Strongly argues that national legislation, not pan‑European self‑regulation, should determine gambling rules, invoking subsidiarity and national sovereignty – explicit ideological commitment.

en: Therefore, the Commission must have an office which would be responsible for approving and allowing the use of these systems on a European scale and which would ensure uniform and effective control at European and national levels.
reason: Advocates creating a Commission office to approve and uniformly control systems across Europe, supporting deeper EU‑level regulatory integration.

en: The result of this simplification would be a reduction in administrative costs for public entities. I also welcome the special attention given to designations of origin and the call on the Commission to ensure that this issue is included on the World Trade Organisation’s agenda.
reason: Supports administrative simplification, protection of designations of origin and bringing the issue to the WTO agenda – a clear position on trade policy and EU product protection.

en: The issue of harmonising and mutually recognising standards with regard to food is very important for ensuring human health. The quality of food products has a fundamental significance to the safety of food for our citizens. Food products must also be properly packed, transported and stored. To ensure good food quality, consumers must also be given complete information on the products they buy, the ingredients, any genetic modifications, the place of manufacture, the storage conditions, how to prepare it and the use by date. The rapporteur favours the introduction of a European service responsible for certification and food quality at Commission level to ensure that minimum certification requirements are met. This would provide a uniform system of control at EU and Member State level. On the basis of an earlier resolution, the report also favours the introduction of a special quality mark for European products.
reason: Calls for EU‑wide harmonisation of food standards, a European certification service and a quality mark, endorsing strong EU regulatory coordination on food safety.

en: At a time when we are facing a serious economic crisis, it is our duty to take measures to support European farmers and processors and ensure that consumers have access to the best products at the most favourable prices. I rather think that the purpose of introducing this mark must be to promote European products and the benefits which they enjoy over those from third countries and to provide European consumers with better information.
reason: Advocates measures to support European farmers and promote European products over third‑country goods, reflecting a protectionist, pro‑EU agricultural policy stance.

en: The essential elements of this process are cooperation between national competition institutions and coordination through the European Competition Network. Based on the criteria of flexibility and pragmatism, the 2006 and 2007 reports give a favourable evaluation of the effectiveness and development of the ECN’s work. The efforts to fund training and judicial cooperation between state judges to interpret EU competition law and ensure its implementation are also welcome.
reason: Expresses approval of cooperation between national competition authorities and the European Competition Network, indicating support for EU‑level competition coordination, though the statement is largely descriptive.

en: The European Commission is to be applauded in its initiatives to date and its continuing work aimed at eliminating red tape for small businesses. Ms Herczog’s report recognises the work done by the Commission and calls for further steps in this direction. This issue is of such importance to Ireland, especially in these economic times, that I had to vote against this proposal.
reason: Praises the Commission’s red‑tape reduction for small businesses but also notes a vote against the proposal; the overall stance on deregulation is ambiguous and weakly expressed.

en: The initiative to create the most favourable conditions for SMEs to obtain funding (risk capital, micro-credits, etc.) is very important. Only complex measures, i.e. promoting higher standards of manufacturing processes and ecological standards for products within the EU, and popularising these same standards throughout the world, as well as enhancing supervision of the EU market, can contribute to common global challenges, such as climate change and diminishing fossil fuel reserves.
reason: Advocates EU‑wide higher ecological and manufacturing standards, stronger market supervision and funding conditions for SMEs to meet climate and energy challenges – a clear policy stance on regulation and environmental protection.

en: That is why the Members representing the Portuguese Social Democratic Party (PSD) are supporting this report, which is, as a matter of fact, coherent with the measures proposed in Portugal by the leader of the PSD, Dr Manuela Ferreira Leite.
reason: Only notes party support for a report without stating any specific political principle or policy position; thus provides no explicit ideological content.

en: The Commission’s proposal for a Small Business Act is part of a communication containing legislative proposals, guiding principles and measures to be implemented to help SMEs in Europe. I welcome the articulation of ten guiding principles which focus on the needs and requirements of SMEs and aim to help them realise their full market potential. Vitally important is the introduction of means of using the present crisis to respond to the environmental crisis by increasing efficiency, through thorough environmental management systems.
reason: Supports a Small Business Act that links SME development with environmental management and crisis response, expressing a clear stance on combining economic support with ecological regulation.

en: In fact, in the name of the 91.5% of businesses in the European Union that employed less than 10 workers in 2003, they want better conditions in order to destroy essential public services, deregulate the labour market and call into question social and working rights.
reason: Strongly opposes deregulation and the weakening of public services, defending social and labour rights; a clear ideological commitment to protecting social welfare against market liberalisation.

en: In this context, and because the present crisis threatens severe economic disruption, we need to implement legal regulations at EU level which will help these enterprises to function. This should, in particular, cover issues such as the transfer of ownership in enterprises (particularly in the case of the illness or retirement of the owner) and for harmonised time limits for the payment of transactions (to avoid ‘credit crunches’). The document also accentuates the importance to these enterprises of innovation, scientific research, patents and inventions and protecting intellectual property, and e-commerce. SMEs should also be assured access to sources of finance, including European funds and credits. Also worthy of mention are the ten principles to guide policy towards small enterprises, both at EU and at Member State level. I also believe that underlining the need to support and promote the activity of SMEs at a cross-border level in the internal market is essential.
reason: Calls for EU‑level legal regulations to aid SMEs (ownership transfer, payment terms, IP, finance), indicating a clear preference for coordinated regulatory support for small enterprises.

en: On a more operational level, it also includes a package of more than 50 separate measures, including four legislative proposals that translate these principles into action. Support for SMEs must be a top priority, particularly in this period of serious economic crisis. Given that most of these actions fall within the competence of the Member States, we need to find ways of involving the Member States and Community bodies in order to guarantee that SMEs can gain added value from the measures affecting them. I also support the idea of having a specific budget line for SMEs…
reason: Emphasises priority support for SMEs, specific EU budget lines and Member State involvement, showing a distinct policy position favouring fiscal and institutional backing of small businesses.

en: Paragraph 68 of this report contains a reference to a common consolidated corporate tax base, stating that there should be a common basis for company taxation.
reason: Explicitly advocates a common consolidated corporate tax base, representing a clear stance on EU tax harmonisation and fiscal integration.

en: The globalisation associated with the current crisis has changed many of the circumstances that served as a basis for decisions taken at European level in the past and which were, at the time, considered correct. Taking this into account, I am convinced that, for example, some aspects of the regional and cohesion policies must be revisited. I therefore support this report, since it is precisely at these moments that we must think about SMEs and their contribution to innovation, economic growth and employment.
reason: Calls for revisiting regional and cohesion policies and stresses the importance of SMEs for innovation and growth, indicating a policy preference for reforming EU structural policies.

en: I cannot agree with a common consolidated corporate tax base as there is no agreement for this.
reason: Expresses clear opposition to a common consolidated corporate tax base, articulating a distinct position against EU‑wide tax harmonisation.

en: We have also succeeded in laying down a fairer, more flexible system of sanctions that is also more effective than the one we had before, since it penalises those who do not act as they should, but it does so according to the severity of the infringement committed and the organisation’s financial means. Finally, we have managed to make progress on the very tricky issue of recognition of classification certificates, by setting out the terms on which recognised organisations will have to recognise each other, but without endangering maritime safety, and taking the most stringent rules as our reference in order to safeguard the standards of excellence that characterise our European naval industries. We have learnt the lessons from our past and realise that we have to act immediately to prevent such things from happening in that way again. Lastly, but no less importantly for all that, I would like to highlight this Chamber’s steadfastness in upholding Europe’s interests and protecting the citizens whom we represent.
reason: Defends stricter, proportionate sanctions, maritime safety standards and European interests, reflecting a strong commitment to EU regulatory strength and protection of citizens.

en: Our ambition was to create an area of responsibility within which each party involved in maritime transport must take its fair share of the responsibility for its choices and actions and, where appropriate, for its errors and mistakes. Today, when this House is being asked to give its opinion on the outcome of a conciliation procedure that will bring a conclusion to this long process – more than three years’ work – we as rapporteurs are delighted with this joint approach, which has enabled us to achieve what I believe to be a very satisfactory result.
reason: The statement praises a joint approach and responsibility sharing but does not advocate a specific political principle or policy; it is largely a generic commendation.

en: All ships must be equipped with AIS, an automatic system that provides information on ships entering European waters, enabling us to locate and contain the risks. We insist once again – and I think that this is important – that the ship’s crew be treated fairly in case of an accident and not erroneously regarded as criminals. We knew already that we needed plans, but now an authority is needed too, one that is not only involved in drawing up these plans but also takes care of their implementation.
reason: Calls for mandatory AIS equipment, fair treatment of crew, and the creation of an implementing authority – a clear stance on safety regulation and labour rights within maritime policy.

en: Certainly, we can now tell our fellow citizens that when they get on board a ship they are covered, in basic terms, from the end of 2012, irrespective of how they travel. To sum up, we have, also from this point of view, enabled all citizens to feel a little more European, since the same cover will apply in any sea, in any location, for any ship.
reason: Advocates uniform passenger coverage across all EU waters, linking it to a stronger European identity; this expresses a firm pro‑EU integration and consumer‑protection principle.

en: I would also say that, in political terms, this is a truly remarkable success for the Community, because the link between the Commission and Parliament has made it possible to produce a very complicated text and piece of legislation about which the Member States were very reticent. We have a number of straits, including the Bosphorus, Gibraltar and Pas-de-Calais – through which 800 commercial ships pass every day – which are among the largest ports on the planet.
reason: Highlights a legislative success for the Community and the Commission‑Parliament link but does not propose a concrete policy; the ideological content is weak and mainly celebratory.

en: This process is more than three years old and, during that time, we have argued strongly for more safety for passengers, oceans, seas and maritime routes. Member States have to make sure that ships which fly their flag and have been detained in the context of a port state inspection are brought into conformity with the relevant IMO conventions. In parallel with the common position, Member States will confirm in a joint declaration their commitment to ratify the main international conventions on maritime safety before 1 January 2012, apply the IMO Flag State Code and the related audit scheme for maritime authorities, and encourage the IMO to make these two instruments mandatory worldwide. My participation in this process was a great honour.
reason: Strongly argues for higher safety standards, ratification of international conventions, and worldwide mandatory IMO rules – a clear commitment to regulatory safety and environmental protection.

en: The citizens perhaps do not understand, sometimes, why we sit for so long and why everything takes so long.
reason: Simply remarks that citizens may not understand procedural delays; no political principle or policy position is expressed.

en: I was in my office listening to Vice-President Tajani and the other speakers, and I feel I have to congratulate all the rapporteurs and the Commission.
reason: Congratulatory comments toward rapporteurs and the Commission without any substantive policy advocacy.

en: In recent years it has largely been the EU that has set the standard for the impact of shipping on the environment through legislation and through the work of the International Maritime Organisation. However, the EU could take the lead and set the standard by demanding more stringent rules. The seven directives in the third maritime package will prevent pollution, ensure a better coordinated response to accidents and prevent poor ships from entering EU waters.
reason: Calls on the EU to lead by imposing stricter environmental rules for shipping, linking it to pollution prevention and coordinated accident response – a strong environmental‑regulation stance.

en: We have special competent bodies to carry out inspections, but we do not have sufficiently clear rules for the seaworthiness of these ships or for when the inspection is to be carried out. Therefore, like Mr Costa, I would like to ask the Commission to extend the provisions on survey and approval to include these types of ship as soon as possible.
reason: Requests clearer seaworthiness rules and extension of survey provisions, indicating a clear demand for tighter regulatory oversight in maritime safety.

en: In the liability regulation in favour of passengers on passenger ships there is, unfortunately, only a regulation for the maritime area.
reason: Notes the limited scope of existing passenger liability regulation but does not explicitly advocate a change; the statement lacks a clear ideological commitment.

en: Along the same lines, how many more maritime and environmental disasters do we need to have before the Commission, the Council and this Parliament will finally turn their attention to the long-standing scandal of flags of convenience? Perhaps, though, it would be wiser for the European electorate to fill Parliament with more MEPs who care more about working for the safety of their fellow citizens than about standing up for free trade, which destroys people and the environment.
reason: Explicitly opposes free‑trade policies, calls for stronger environmental and safety regulation and for MEPs who prioritize citizen safety over free‑trade, showing a clear ideological stance on market regulation and environmental protection.

en: What happens if it then results in a serious incident, closing a major port?
reason: Only asks a rhetorical question about a possible incident; no political principle or policy position is expressed.

en: I should like to congratulate the rapporteur, Mr Sterckx, and the entire negotiating team on achieving a valuable compromise on this important issue. To close, I welcome the fact that Parliament's actions have pushed the Council into adopting a final common position on all seven legislative proposals in the package.
reason: Praises a compromise and the legislative process without advocating any substantive policy; generic commendation, not ideological.

en: Another consistent step forward is the requirement for ships to be insured by financial guarantee certificates, which will put real responsibility on their charterers. Finally, I would like to pay tribute to the work that has been done in this field by Mr Tajani, who is here today, and the rapporteurs on transport law, because we have now embarked on the final stages of the process on maritime law with the aim of covering all transport in Europe.
reason: Mentions insurance requirements and responsibility for charterers, but does not explicitly argue for a broader political principle; weak regulatory signal.

en: Since then, we in the Committee on Transport and Tourism have worked on a succession of legislative packages in an attempt to overcome the excessive resistance we have encountered among shipowners, oil companies, classification societies and also certain Member States, which rejected the three proposals for being too stringent. I trust it will not take another 10 years to control illegal discharges at sea more effectively and efficiently.
reason: Criticises resistance from industry and some Member States and urges faster control of illegal discharges, indicating a preference for stricter environmental regulation, though the stance is moderate.

en: The measures relating to maritime transport must be supplemented by increasing cooperation between littoral states in order to make the most efficient use of resources and reduce the pollution resulting from activities carried out in ports and on shore, as well as along the whole course of the Danube. The Black Sea can only be protected effectively through concerted action in every area.
reason: Calls for increased cooperation among littoral states to reduce pollution and protect the Black Sea, expressing a clear commitment to regional environmental cooperation and collective governance.

en: There has been much negotiation and debate, and I am glad to see the issues have been finally resolved. The adoption of this package is a victory for the European Parliament and certainly for the rapporteurs who have fought to ensure that we delivered on behalf of our citizens, even against very strong opposition from Member State governments.
reason: Frames the legislative adoption as a victory for the European Parliament against Member State opposition, signalling a pro‑EU, parliamentary‑centric view of governance.

en: In the case of the Black Sea in particular, this package will be particularly important as many of the Black Sea littoral states are on the Paris Memorandum blacklist or grey list. However, the way in which these services are paid for must be clearly regulated.
reason: Advocates clear regulation of how services are paid for, indicating a regulatory preference but without a broader ideological context.

en: This package is a testament to the work of Parliament, the Commission and also, if belatedly, the Council.
reason: Simply acknowledges the work of EU institutions; no specific policy position or principle is articulated.

en: I think that that is a sign to everyone involved that this is not an ideological conflict but rather is a matter of making practical arrangements to improve maritime safety. I should also like to thank the Commissioner for his answer to my question on the uncertainty over the agency and its role. Now then, I welcome the consensus, and am also proud of what we have achieved, but I do think, Commissioner – as both you and Mrs Vlasto have already said – that everything now depends on the quality of the implementation. We shall keep an eye on you, and shall support you again if further proposals are needed.
reason: Emphasises practical implementation over ideological conflict; no explicit political principle is presented.

en: I also think it would be good for the Commission to report to Parliament on this subject in 2012.
reason: A generic suggestion that the Commission report to Parliament; no clear political principle or ideological stance is expressed.

en: Means of legal recourse exist that are sufficiently clear, accessible and based on information that is clear and available in advance. As I have already said, the adoption of this third maritime safety package is a significant victory for the European legislative process. The Commission, the Council and Parliament have accepted a text that improves everyone’s lives, promotes better security on the seas, oceans and inland waters, and prepares our future.
reason: Praises a maritime safety package and the legislative process, hinting at support for rule‑of‑law and safety regulation, but the statement remains vague and lacks a concrete policy position.

en: The vote will take place tomorrow.
reason: Simply states that a vote will occur; contains no ideological content.

en: By adopting this, the European Parliament will set a new benchmark in terms of standards for investigating accidents involving vessels.
reason: Mentions setting a new benchmark for accident investigations, which suggests a preference for higher safety standards, yet it does not articulate a broader political principle.

en: I have also read that we mean to make road pricing compulsory for all passenger cars in Europe. With the help of the majority in the Committee on Transport and Tourism, we managed to draft a balanced, reasonable, coherent proposal. Firstly, which externalities are to be introduced into the system? Consequently, I wish to propose to my fellow Members that we stick with the package supported by the Committee on Transport and Tourism.
reason: Advocates compulsory road pricing and internalising externalities, reflecting a clear stance on market‑based environmental regulation and EU‑wide transport policy.

en: That is why the European Community quite simply needs an infrastructure that meets its needs and equitable transport rules for all modes of transport. Given that transport also has negative consequences for people and the environment, it must, of course, be further greened, in order, also, to play its role in fighting climate change. You cannot just pick out road transport – and, in fact, specifically only goods vehicle traffic – and then say ‘we will leave it up to the Member States to decide whether or not they want to have road tolls.’ My group agrees with the other groups that exhaust emissions and noise should be taken account of in the external costs and in the charging thereof.
reason: Calls for EU‑wide equitable, green transport rules, internalising external costs, and stronger climate action, demonstrating a strong ideological commitment to environmental regulation and supranational governance.

en: The second aspect relates to technology and exports. If Europe introduces a relevant Eurovignette system, it will also promote the rise of European economic players.
reason: Supports the introduction of a Eurovignette system to boost European economic actors, indicating a moderate policy preference for EU‑level transport pricing.

en: The transport sector is one of the key sectors contributing to the European Union’s economic and social development. At the request of the European Parliament, the European Commission proposed internalising external costs and amending the Eurovignette Directive. Although the texts being proposed by the Commission mark a step forward in the development of transport which respects and protects the environment, they can and must be improved. This is why I consider that the process of internalising external costs must be applied to every kind of transport and double taxation must be avoided. Member States must invest in the construction of motorways, high-speed railway lines and in those alternatives which can cut traffic congestion.
reason: Demands internalisation of external costs across all transport modes, avoidance of double taxation, and EU investment in infrastructure, showing a robust ideological position on environmental policy and EU coordination.

en: Therefore, we agree to the inclusion of air pollution, noise and congestion in the internalisation of external costs.
reason: Expresses agreement to include air pollution, noise and congestion in cost internalisation, reflecting a clear environmental regulatory stance.

en: That means that we need new, targeted measures in order to provide a better framework for a market that has come off the rails.
reason: Calls for new, targeted measures to reform a malfunctioning market, indicating a firm position on market regulation and economic governance.

en: As far as my group is concerned, the objective must be to give the most environmentally-friendly modes of transport – transport by rail and water – more of a chance, and to curb the most environmentally damaging – road and air transport.
reason: Advocates a clear environmental transport policy – prioritising rail and water over road and air – indicating a stable commitment to sustainable mobility.

en: I am fairly pleased with the result, and very pleased with the cooperation with the rapporteur. I propose that we return to the old text from 2006, therefore, and I ask for your support for this. On a final note, it is of the utmost importance that the Commission ensures that the Member States do not use this directive to impose unduly high charges on freight transport.
reason: Calls for Member States to internalise polluter costs while limiting excessive charges, showing a definite stance on cost‑internalisation and regulation of the transport sector.

en: In closing, I would like to say that I find it very regrettable that the Czech Presidency has not deemed it worth the effort to send a representative to Parliament for this important legislative proposal.
reason: Expresses disappointment about procedural attendance; no explicit political principle or policy preference is articulated.

reason: Makes a vague comment about procedural delay without endorsing or opposing a concrete political principle.

reason: States that toll decisions should be left to Member States, hinting at a subsidiarity/sovereignty view but without a clear advocacy or opposition.

reason: Opposes external‑cost charges on road hauliers, arguing for protection of small businesses and rejecting the Commission’s proposal – a clear economic‑regulation position.

en: Those who vote ‘no’ on this issue are giving up on climate change and setting our children and our children’s children on the road to ruin, as they will have no future on this planet. We need regulation that is much tougher than what the Commission and the majority of this House have proposed.
reason: Strongly condemns any ‘no’ vote as abandoning climate action and demands tougher regulation, reflecting an explicit, firm climate‑change ideological commitment.

en: We know that measures aiming to combat pollution or stimulate technological innovation, such as cleaner engines and intelligent vehicles, are essential.
reason: Declares that pollution‑combating and innovation measures are essential, indicating a clear policy preference for environmental regulation and technology development.

reason: Highlights the Parliament’s historical call for internalising external costs across all transport modes, affirming a consistent stance on polluter‑pay principles.

en: Excluding CO from the Eurovignette would be particularly unfair given that all Member States now have binding CO reduction targets to meet under the effort-sharing decision.
reason: Calls exclusion of CO from the Eurovignette unfair given EU CO‑reduction targets, advocating alignment of pricing mechanisms with climate commitments.

reason: Explicitly opposes the EPP’s decision to exempt heavy‑goods traffic from paying for CO‑emissions, advocating the polluter‑pays principle and regulatory cost internalisation – a clear environmental‑policy stance.

reason: Highlights the competitive disadvantage of EU carriers due to weaker regulation, implying a need for regulatory parity and market fairness – a clear stance on competition policy.

en: The tolls paid by heavy vehicles to use road infrastructures will support, in the long term, the huge investments in the infrastructures included in the European and national economic recovery plans, at the level of both Trans-European transport networks and of other categories of road infrastructures, including mountainous regions where, in many cases, it is particularly difficult to construct roads. reason: Calls for tolls to fund EU and national infrastructure, urges Commission support, and stresses coordination of spatial and traffic planning – a strong endorsement of EU‑level investment and environmental cost internalisation.

en: I therefore think that we should support the initiative of our erstwhile Belgian colleague.
reason: Only a vague endorsement of an unspecified initiative; no concrete political principle or policy position is articulated.

en: We are currently at a turning point, where we are trying to safeguard our industry whilst making it more sustainable, and to reach the ‘three times 20’ objective that was reaffirmed by the President of the European Union at the time, Nicolas Sarkozy, in this House last December.
